title: Tracing the origins of St Helena's liberated Africans

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full Zenodo deposit (143,045 bytes, CC-BY-4.0, mirror of GitHub XY2025-Archaeology/StHelena_isotope, MIT licence) and opened all 5 Excel files plus the 4 R scripts. Counted: Data S2 = 193 enamel 87Sr/86Sr measurements on 152 unique individuals across 117 burial groups, zero missing cells, values 0.712776-0.772541 with a 2SE (two standard errors) column; Data S4 = 337 published measurements from 12 African-diaspora burial sites in 7 countries; Data S5 = 559 laser-ablation points along 11 tooth transects; Data S3 = 3 animal teeth; Data S1 = 18 rows of ship-arrival counts by port. Confirmed by reading Fig.3.R and Fig.2B&4C.R that geographic origin is produced at runtime by assignR::pdRaster applied to an external raster (panaf_model_repeatedCV.tif, the Wang et al. 2024 random-forest isoscape), which is not in the deposit.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The article itself is paywalled (Europe PMC isOpenAccess=N, science.org returned HTTP 403), so the interpretation of which homelands were inferred, the integration with ancient DNA, and the reburial decision come from the abstract and press coverage only. The Wang et al. 2024 pan-African isoscape (2,266 environmental samples, figshare) was read about in search results, not opened.

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.19605943, CC-BY-4.0, 143 KB zip, no login; I downloaded and extracted it.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. There is no origin/homeland column anywhere in the 5 sheets. The thing to predict (where a person grew up) must be constructed by running a Bayesian assignment (assignR) against an external isoscape raster; the 'Regions/Country' column in Data S4 is the burial site, not the African origin.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are present as values: 87Sr/86Sr ratio, 2SE, tooth type, age-at-death band, sex, dental modification, burial group, Sr concentration in ppm for 12 individuals.

a4_units_stated.note: 87Sr/86Sr is a dimensionless isotope ratio with an explicit 2SE column; Sr concentration labelled ppm (parts per million); every sheet has a title line stating what it is.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. 193 enamel measurements on 152 individuals, counted in Data S2. Even pooling the 337 published diaspora measurements in Data S4 gives 530 rows, and those come from other labs with no origin label either. Far below the ~1,500-row bar.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially fits; the only large object would be the external isoscape raster, which is not in this deposit.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Abstract says 152 individuals; Data S2 has exactly 152 unique individual IDs and 193 measurements, matching the press description of 193 measurements.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL by circularity. Any origin label would be the output of the Wang et al. 2024 random-forest strontium isoscape plus an assignR posterior, i.e. another model's prediction, and it is computed directly from the single feature (87Sr/86Sr) we would be modelling. No individual here has a documented birthplace.

existing_models.name: Wang et al. 2024 pan-African bioavailable strontium isoscape (random-forest regression over environmental rasters, Nature Communications 15:10891)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported from repeated cross-validation over 2,266 environmental samples; I saw this in search-result summaries, not in the paper itself, so I have no verified R-squared or RMSE (root mean squared error) number.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Search summaries state that local sampling is needed to improve local accuracy, i.e. large parts of Africa are sparsely sampled; I did not read the discussion directly.

existing_models.name: assignR (R package implementing Bayesian geographic assignment from isotope values to an isoscape)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a trained model; it converts an isoscape plus its error map into a per-individual probability surface. This is exactly what the St Helena paper runs.

existing_models.name: Bataille et al. 2018 bioavailable strontium isoscape for Western Europe (machine-learning / random forest, PLOS One)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search summary says random-forest regression outperformed other regression and interpolation methods; no split or number verified by me.

existing_models.name: Bioavailable strontium isoscape of Angola (machine-learning framework with local plant sampling, Journal of Archaeological Science 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to improve on the global isoscape prediction for Angola; no number verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Local sampling density is the limiting factor, per the search summary.

backbone.name: None applicable
backbone.hardware: CPU only; the data is a 143 KB spreadsheet

integration.partner_dataset: Wang et al. 2024 pan-African strontium isoscape and its 2,266 environmental baseline samples (figshare), plus WorldClim/geology rasters
integration.join_key: geographic coordinates (WGS84) and the 87Sr/86Sr value itself
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could a better-calibrated isoscape narrow the plausible homelands of trafficked individuals enough to name a region rather than a continent-scale band? — but that question is answered with the isoscape paper's data, not with this paper's 193 unlabelled measurements.

controls.positive_control: The three animal teeth in Data S3 (two rabbits, one rat, 0.7078-0.7083) are a local St Helena baseline that any assignment must place on the island, not in Africa — a genuine control, but only 3 rows.
controls.negative_control: None runnable: with no ground-truth origin there is nothing to shuffle against.
controls.external_validation: The 337 published diaspora measurements in Data S4 are a second source of values but also have no known origins, so they validate the distribution, not an assignment.

honest_claim_h3: Any model built on this file could only claim 'this is the probability surface implied by the 2024 random-forest isoscape for a given enamel 87Sr/86Sr value', which restates the published method rather than testing it, because not one of the 152 individuals has a documented birthplace.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use tooth enamel strontium isotope ratios to predict which African region a trafficked person grew up in.
plain_idea.train_on: What is actually in the files: 193 enamel 87Sr/86Sr measurements on 152 individuals buried at Rupert's Valley, St Helena, each with age-at-death band, sex, tooth type, dental modification and burial group; plus 559 laser-ablation points along 11 teeth and 337 published measurements from other diaspora burials.
plain_idea.predict: The intended output is a childhood homeland region. The true answer does not exist: nobody recorded where these individuals were born, and the paper's 'answer' is itself a probability map produced by a random-forest isoscape plus a Bayesian assignment step.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: The question matters enormously to the St Helena community and to descendant communities, and the paper shows the method informing a real reburial decision — but the value here is in the measurements and the isoscape, not in a supervised learning task this table can support.

more_or_better_data.why: 193 measurements on 152 individuals versus the 2,266 environmental samples behind the existing pan-African isoscape; and ours carry no location, which is the only thing that would make them training data.

confidence_score.why: Each measurement has a 2SE of roughly 0.00001, so analytical noise is known, but the existing assignR workflow already propagates isoscape uncertainty into a per-individual probability surface, which is a calibrated confidence by construction.

models_beatable.why: The incumbent is a 2024 random forest evaluated by repeated cross-validation with open code and data on figshare, and this paper is by the same first author, so it is both current and already the state of the art for this region.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The condition that fails first is the evaluation split: there is no held-out set of individuals with known origins, so neither the baseline nor a new model can be scored at all.

ml_idea: The only defensible ML idea nearby is not in this paper: train a bioavailable 87Sr/86Sr regression on the Wang et al. 2024 pan-African environmental baseline (2,266 samples with coordinates, on figshare) using geology, climate and soil rasters, and test spatial generalisation with geographically blocked cross-validation. This paper's 152 individuals would then serve only as an application demo, not as training data.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed beyond the actual download and parse: the whole deposit is 143 KB and all five sheets loaded into pandas in under a second.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open Data S2 and look for an origin column, then count rows: there is none, and there are 193 rows for 152 people. Two minutes.

verdict_reason: Three Part A killers. A2: no origin label exists as a column — the paper's answer is a probability surface computed at runtime by assignR from an external isoscape raster that is not even in the deposit. A8: that label is therefore another model's output, computed from the single feature we would model, which is textbook circularity. A5: 193 measurements on 152 individuals is an order of magnitude below the threshold. The data itself is exemplary — clean, complete, CC-BY-4.0, units stated, counts matching the abstract — and the study is genuinely important, but it is a provenance application of an existing random-forest isoscape, not a supervised learning dataset. If the strontium thread is worth pursuing, the candidate to evaluate is the Wang et al. 2024 pan-African isoscape baseline (2,266 georeferenced environmental samples on figshare), where the label is a measured value at a known location.
